newsitem.title: USA: IBM raises dividend, shareholders ebullient.
newsitem.headline: IBM raises dividend, shareholders ebullient.

text.p: International Business Machines Corp. raised its dividend 14 percent and boosted its stock buyback plan Tuesday as Chairman Louis Gerstner said he wasn't through remaking the world's largest computer maker.

The dividend increase, the second by IBM in less than a year, delighted shareholders, who voted at the company's annual meeting here to approve a 2-for-1 stock split announced on Jan. 28, IBM's first split since 1979.
Industry analysts said the latest moves by IBM -- whose stock is one of the most widely held in the United States -- were clear signals of management's confidence in the future.

"This is obviously a vote of confidence by management in the prospects for this company," said William Milton at Brown Brothers Harriman. "If the company were not confident of its prospects, it wouldn't be making this kind of commitment."

IBM raised its quarterly dividend 5 cents to 40 cents a share after it raised the payout 5 cents last June. It also earmarked another $3.5 billion to buy back its stock, after buying back $2 billion worth in the first quarter.
Many shareholders congratulated Gerstner after he addressed his fourth IBM annual meeting for his work turning around the company.
"A lot has happened in four years," Gerstner told the meeting. "As most of you know -- because you lived through it as shareholders -- IBM was in critical condition."
Gerstner, who joined IBM in 1993, noted IBM lost $16 billion from 1991 through 1993. The company has shed 117,000 jobs and wrote off $28 billion for restructuring.

Last week it reported first-quarter earnings that beat expectations on Wall Street and sent its stock soaring, and the stock rose again after Tuesday's announcements, adding $8 to $158.375 in active trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
"Our transformation is far, far, from finished," Gerstner said, but added that "IBM is an exciting place to work again."
He noted IBM's stock price has more than tripled since hitting a low of $40.375 in August 1993.
Some of the 900 shareholders at the meeting expressed pleasure with the dividend increase, though the payout remains far from IBM's previous high payout of $1.21 a quarter.

"We'd like for it to be more, naturally," said Margaret Tyree, a shareholder from outside Oklahoma City. "But it's in the best interest of the company" not to raise it too much, she said, adding that she and her husband Lee, a retired IBM employee, thought Gerstner was doing a great job.

The dividend increase and buyback answered questions about what IBM would do with its $6.4 billion in cash on hand and could help it retain the momentum it recently recaptured on Wall Street, analysts said.
"They're clearly signalling they want to stay more aggressive with the share repurchase programme," said John Jones at Salomon Brothers. "That should help earnings per share a lot."
The effects of previous buybacks were evident in IBM's first-quarter earnings, which rose to $2.37 a share from $2.21 even as net income was little changed at $1.19 billion.

Gerstner said that after he took the helm in April 1993, many people advised him to "get rid" of IBM's older businesses, such as mainframe computers, since their steep decline contributed to IBM's financial woes.
But customers said they needed mainframes to run their businesses so IBM cut prices and made them compatible with other computer systems customers needed, Gerstner said.
And the industry shift to using large machines known as servers to store data and run massive computer networks has also helped. "We got lucky," he said.

"They're good generators of cash, but growth is a challenge," he said, referring to IBM's mainframes, AS/400 minicomputers and mainframe software. He said hardware revenues will grow again after being basically flat in the first quarter.
Gerstner said IBM's services business -- the bright spot in its stronger-than-expected first quarter earnings -- will continue to grow faster than the industry.

"If you pull back from the trees and look at IBM's forest, I think you see a company that has made solid progress in repositioning our large established businesses, while investing aggressively in new growth areas," Gerstner said.

"It was evident that shareholders were pleased and he was playing to a partisan crowd," said industry consultant Sam Albert, who attended the meeting. "Compared with 1993, the turnaround in the audience reaction mirrored the turnaround of the company."
